description: Hi! We’re Team CrescentSphere, and we’re interested in AI, space exploration, and design. We’re looking for creative and motivated teammates to help create a working project.
summary: We built CrescentSphere, a free web app that lets anyone compare lunar landing sites and dates in seconds. Pick one of 59 curated sites, or click any point on the Moon, choose a date, and drop into a 3D surface view showing where the Sun and Earth sit against the real terrain horizon, with live countdowns to sunset and Earthset. Pinning up to four site-and-date scenarios compares power and communication side by side, and a heatmap shows where the Sun and Earth are both visible. A south pole terrain viewer shows steep slopes, deep craters and their shadows from real NASA elevation data. Our Monte Carlo planner simulates about 55,000 Earth-to-Moon flights for a chosen landing date and recommends the best site and route, requiring both Sun and Earth to be visible. Positions come from JPL Horizons and terrain from NASA LOLA, for any coordinate on the Moon. This matters because a small change in site or date can decide whether a lander has power and a direct link to Earth. CrescentSphere turns the data in Quickmap, Moon Trek and Horizons into one clear tool for planners, educators and the public.
details:
CrescentSphere is an interactive 3D simulation and decision-support tool that lets users evaluate lunar landing sites and dates for solar power and direct-to-Earth communication. Built with JavaScript, three.js, and Python, the system opens on the Earth and Moon at true scale, lets the user select a site and a date, and computes where the Sun and Earth sit relative to the horizon from that exact spot, taking the surrounding terrain into account.

How It Works:
The app presents each site-date combination three ways: a 3D surface view the user can look around in, a 60-day timeline showing when the Sun and Earth are above the horizon, and a heatmap of the whole Moon showing where both are visible at once. Sun, Earth, and Moon positions come from JPL Horizons, and the terrain comes from NASA LOLA elevation data, ray-marched to find the horizon while accounting for the Moon’s curvature. A Monte Carlo planner works in the opposite direction: given a landing date, it simulates a large set of random Earth-to-Moon flights, scores them on fuel and on days of continuous Sun and Earth after landing, and recommends the best site and route.

Benefits:

  • Faster Comparison: Mission teams can test “what if we slip a week?” in one tool instead of moving between Quickmap, Moon Trek, and Horizons.
  • Traceable Accuracy: Every value comes from NASA data, and our sunrise, sunset, Earthrise, and Earthset times are checked against Horizons’ own output.
  • Accessibility: Explorer mode gives students and the public a visual view, while Researcher mode gives planners azimuth, elevation, libration, horizon profiles, and CSV export.
  • Real Terrain Anywhere: Any coordinate on the Moon loads real LOLA terrain, so users are not limited to a fixed list of sites.

Intended Impact:
CrescentSphere is meant to shorten the time it takes a mission team to find a workable alternative when a launch date or landing site changes, and to help educators and the public see why the Moon’s south pole is such a hard place to land.

Development Tools and Technology Stack:

  • Frontend: JavaScript (ES modules), HTML, CSS, three.js, GLSL shaders on WebGL2
  • Computation: Web Workers for the whole-Moon illumination heatmaps
  • Data Pipelines: Python 3 with NumPy and SciPy to cut and tile LOLA data and fetch Horizons data
  • Data Sources: JPL Horizons API, NASA LOLA elevation grids
  • Hosting: Firebase Hosting, as a static site with no backend or build step
  • Development Hardware: Mac laptops, with an AI coding assistant.

Creativity and Innovation:
The project’s creativity lies in bringing the whole planning problem into one continuous scene. A user can fly from Earth to a crater, land, watch the Sun rise over the real terrain horizon, and then see the Monte Carlo flights fan out toward the winning route. Terrain is fully loaded before a site is displayed.

Design Considerations:

  • Physical Accuracy: With no atmosphere there is no refraction, so the horizon is set only by terrain and the Moon’s curvature. We modeled libration, Earth’s parallax from the site, the Sun’s real angular size, and Earth passing in front of the Sun, and used the Sun’s upper limb to match Horizons.
  • Real NASA Terrain at Every Scale: 59 sites use LOLA terrain at 30–100 m, and global LOLA tiles extend real elevation data to every coordinate on the Moon. A user can click anywhere and stand on measured ground.
  • Portability: A static site that runs on a laptop or a classroom screen.
  • Audience: Two interface modes so one tool serves both specialists and the public.
